<scenario>
<description>An adopter that wants a de facto exemption for their favorite workload creates a brand-new party artefact declaring the `platform` role for a Namespace that has nothing to do with real infrastructure — e.g. `namespaces.yaml` for a marketing analytics Namespace gets tagged `posture.acme.io/tier: infra` and the party.yaml for that team is edited (in an otherwise unreviewed side-repo or a less-scrutinized adopter fork) to carry `role: platform`. Since `distribution/verify-infra-declaration.sh` only checks that platform-role parties asserting `infra` are consistent, and role-granting itself isn't gated by any body described in this ADR beyond "a party with the platform role," a team that controls its own party.yaml (or slips a PR past reviewers who don't recognize the significance of a `role:` field bump) gets its Namespace onto the tightest-looking-but-actually-most-privileged rung, `infra`, bypassing the entire priced ladder (`baseline→isolated`) with a single self-declared role change.</description>
<explanation>The code (ADR-0022 §"infra is a declaration, not a selection" and "Only a party with the `platform` role may declare... infra") never specifies who grants the `platform` role or what governs party.yaml itself — it's treated as ambient truth. This is a governance gap: nothing in the code prevents a party from unilaterally asserting its own `platform` role to escape the priced conditional-policy ladder (Principle 4) via a self-serving declaration rather than meeting conditions everyone else must meet, which is exactly the "favour"/carve-out Principle 3 and 13 forbid (must be resolved by open PR to policy, not silent self-declaration).</explanation>
</scenario>

<scenario>
<description>A workload owner wants no cage at all. They deploy their pod into a Namespace that is deliberately never labeled `governed: "true"` and never given any tier — fully ungoverned. Per the 2026-09-04 flip, an ungoverned Namespace now renders `isolated`. But the owner also ensures the pod carries no `policy-as-versioned.dev/policy-version` claim and that no `cage-tier` MutatingPolicy is scoped to watch that Namespace at all (e.g., it's a Namespace created outside the platform's Namespace-discovery mechanism, in a cluster region the composed artefact doesn't enumerate). Since the mutation only reaches Namespaces the policy's `namespaceObject` selector/watch actually covers, a Namespace invisible to that selector never gets mutated to `isolated` in practice — it just runs completely uncaged, indefinitely, as long as it stays off whatever list the platform's discovery uses to generate watched Namespaces.</description>
<explanation>Principle 2 and Article "an unknown or unlabelled tier fails closed to isolated" assume universal coverage/admission, but the code's actual mechanism (`cage-tier` reading `namespaceObject`, watched Namespaces) depends on discovery/enumeration that isn't specified as exhaustive. A Namespace that never enters the discovery surface is a workload that is never caged at all rather than caged tightly — silence doesn't "buy the bottom rung" as promised in Principle 7, it buys total invisibility, violating "everything is always caged" (Principle 1).</explanation>
</scenario>

<scenario>
<description>An adopter unhappy with the `isolated` bottom rung for its Namespace doesn't lower via the priced floor mechanism. Instead, each sprint they simply delete and recreate the governed Namespace with a brand-new name (e.g. `payments-v47`, `payments-v48`...), each time submitting a *fresh* Namespace manifest with tier `baseline` — since a newly created Namespace has no history of a prior tighter declaration, `tighten-only` (Article 8, "never writes... looser than declared") only binds *within* a Namespace's own lineage, not across a rename/recreate. The tier_binding.py check compares `proposed_tier` to the Namespace's current label, but a fresh Namespace object has no prior committed tier to compare against, so the "never looser than the party's worst-priced regime" rule (which is scoped to prices[] fold logic, not cross-Namespace memory) never fires against the old, tighter `payments-v46`.</description>
<explanation>Article 10/11 say the tier is bound to the party's worst-priced regime and floors are tighten-only, but nothing in the code tracks tier history across Namespace identity churn — "the declaration can never be looser than the party's worst-priced regime" is enforced per-Namespace-name, not per-party-lineage. This lets a party launder away an accumulated tight tier by simply renaming its Namespace, which is functionally an exemption via technical workaround, violating Principle 3 (no exemptions) and Principle 11 (floor lowering must be priced, never a free reset).</explanation>
</scenario>

<scenario>
<description>An on-call SRE, during a live production incident, creates an emergency debugging Namespace to run a pod with `tcpdump`/packet capture tools to diagnose a cascading network failure that's taking down customer-facing services. They don't have time to properly declare a tier or go through the platform team's onboarding flow for a new Namespace — they just `kubectl create namespace incident-2026-09-21` and drop a pod in to capture traffic before the failure window closes. Because the Namespace is ungoverned/untiered, the pod lands on `isolated`: no egress, no ingress, first eviction. The debugging pod can't reach the network it needs to inspect, and gets evicted mid-capture, right when it might have identified the root cause.</description>
<explanation>Under the flipped default (ticket 63) and the ordering rule, an ungoverned or unlabelled Namespace renders `isolated` — "silence buys nothing anywhere" (principle 7). This is a blanket, tighten-only, no-exception rule (principle 3: no exemptions). Morally, however, a good-faith emergency responder acting to restore service and prevent customer harm is exactly the kind of Good Samaritan case where rigid rule-following (no fast-path for incident namespaces) actively worsens the outcome, and no amount of "conditional policy" exists yet for this urgent, legitimate use.</explanation>
</scenario>

<scenario>
<description>A platform engineer needs to temporarily lower a team's Namespace floor from `restricted` to `baseline` to let a security researcher run an authorized penetration test that requires broader syscalls and network reach, with the change reverted the same day after the test completes. Lowering the floor is priced, not refused (principle 11) — but pricing here means going through the full priced-and-argued residual/pull-request pipeline (per the 2026-09-04 note: "loosening is not implemented... a human edit... under the binding check"). There is no fast lawful path to a same-day temporary loosening; the only lawful mechanism is a human PR edit reviewed in the open, which for a scheduled, pre-approved, time-boxed pentest window is bureaucratically incompatible with the test's schedule.</description>
<explanation>The code states outright that "loosening is not implemented, and that is the decision, not an omission" — any looser declaration must be a manual, reviewed PR edit, with no expedited or time-boxed mechanism (2026-09-04 note). This effectively prohibits legitimate, pre-authorized, time-limited security testing from happening on schedule, even though such testing is professionally required and mutually agreed. The rigidity here chills a valuable, authorized security practice by giving it no faster lawful channel than an unbounded-latency PR review, contradicting the spirit of principle 4 (conditional policy for anyone meeting conditions).</explanation>
</scenario>

<scenario>
<description>A new engineer, unfamiliar with the `policy-as-versioned.dev/policy-version` claim requirement, deploys a harmless internal documentation-site pod into an already-governed, `baseline`-tiered Namespace, simply forgetting to add the version-claim annotation. There's no malicious intent or attempted opt-out — just an oversight in a YAML template. Under `governed-namespace-requires-claim`'s current MutatingPolicy behavior, this pod is silently dropped onto the bottom rung (`isolated`, no ingress/egress, first-eviction priority), causing the docs site to become instantly unreachable and get evicted, with no error message indicating why beyond an obscure label diff.</description>
<explanation>Per the 2026-09-05 amendment, any pod in a governed Namespace lacking the version claim "lands on the BOTTOM RUNG" — "silence is not an exemption and it is not a refusal either; silence is the bottom rung" (principle 7). This treats an innocent clerical omission identically to a deliberate policy-version-orphan evasion attempt (the very abuse the policy was designed to stop). Morally, this overreach catches ordinary human error with the harshest possible outcome and no distinguishable warning, chilling legitimate routine deployment work rather than targeting the adversarial behavior the rule was written for.</explanation>
</scenario>

<reasoning>
The gap is real: ADR-0022 defines behavior conditional on "a party with the `platform` role" but never specifies where that role assertion is authoritative. Since `party.yaml` is adopter-controlled (per the scenario), a self-serving role bump lets any party grant itself the platform role, which is functionally identical to the banned exemption/carve-out (Principle 3) — a named party getting privileged treatment nobody else can get without meeting the same conditions (Principle 4).

This is fixable without touching the tier ladder, the tighten-only mutation logic, the `infra`-is-a-declaration reasoning, or any of the fold/selection rules — all of which stay untouched. The fix is structural: it establishes where role truth lives, consistent with Principle 13 (disagreement/changes go through open PR review) and Principle 9-10 (declarations must be checked against a governed, non-forgeable source, same logic already applied to tier labels being "output only" and Namespace-scoped rather than pod-scoped). The `platform` role should be asserted from a single hub-maintained, reviewed roster (e.g., a signed `platform/roles.yaml` or the hub's own composed artefact), not read from each adopter's freely-editable `party.yaml`. `distribution/verify-infra-declaration.sh` (or a new check alongside it) should validate the `platform` role claim against that hub roster, not merely check self-consistency between an unverified role field and the `infra` tag.

No previously resolved case exists to conflict with, and the revision is a direct extension of the same "declaration must come from a governed, checked source, not a forgeable/self-asserted field" pattern already used for pod tier labels (Principle 9) and infra declarations generally. This is a minimal, principled addition, not a hack.
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Add to ADR-0022, in the "`infra` is a declaration, not a selection" section: 

"The `platform` role itself is not self-declarable in an adopter's own `party.yaml`. It is granted only by entry in a hub-maintained, signed roster (`platform/roles.yaml` or equivalent composed artefact under the hub's own release process, per ADR-0025/point 13's open-PR-to-policy rule), changeable only by a reviewed pull request against the hub repo — never by an adopter-side edit, side-repo, or fork. `distribution/verify-infra-declaration.sh` is extended: before checking self-consistency between a party's declared role and its `infra` tag, it resolves the party's `platform` role claim against the hub roster (not the party's own `party.yaml`) and fails the check if the roster does not list that party as `platform`. A `party.yaml` claiming `role: platform` without a matching hub roster entry renders as `isolated` — the same fallback already specified for a non-platform party declaring `infra` — because an unverifiable role claim is exactly the 'unknown/unlabelled' case Principle 7 already resolves to the bottom rung."
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The loophole exists because ADR-0022 conditions the `infra` rung on "a party with the `platform` role" without ever anchoring where that role is authoritatively granted, letting an adopter self-assert it in their own editable `party.yaml`. The fix requires the `platform` role to be sourced from a hub-maintained, reviewed roster rather than the adopter's own artefact, and treats an unverifiable role claim the same way the code already treats any unlabelled/unverifiable declaration — folding to `isolated`. This closes the self-declared-exemption gap using the same non-forgeable-source and fail-closed patterns already established elsewhere in the code, without altering any ladder, tier, or mutation logic.
</resolution_summary>

<reasoning>
The gap here is purely mechanical: the doctrine says "everything is always caged" and "unlabelled fails closed to isolated," but the described implementation relies on a curated/enumerated discovery list (`namespaceObject` watch scoped to known Namespaces) rather than a cluster-scoped, exhaustive admission mechanism. That's an implementation bug relative to the stated principle, not a conflict between principles or prior cases. Nothing in the resolved doctrine requires discovery to be non-exhaustive — quite the opposite, principle 1 and the tighten-only/fail-closed architecture presuppose universal coverage. Kubernetes-native `MutatingPolicy`/admission webhooks can be scoped with a `namespaceSelector: {}` (match-all) or equivalent cluster-scoped rule rather than an enumerated allowlist, closing exactly this hole without touching any tier-selection logic, floor logic, infra-role logic, or any previously decided ADR content. This is a coverage/enforcement-surface fix, not a change to any ranking, ladder, or exemption rule, so it cannot contradict any resolved case (there are none yet, and it doesn't touch the substantive tier semantics of the current ADR either).

The fix: specify that Namespace admission coverage must be a cluster-scoped, unconditional match (webhook `namespaceSelector: {}`/equivalent "match all Namespace objects", not a maintained enumeration or discovery list), and add a periodic reconciliation control (or admission-time guarantee via the API server's webhook registration itself, which is inherently exhaustive unless explicitly excluded) verifying that every Namespace object in the cluster has a corresponding cage-tier-mutated pod population — closing the specific loophole of "regions the composed artefact doesn't enumerate."
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Add to the "cage ladder" ADR, in the section describing `cage-tier`'s mechanism:

"Coverage is a property of the webhook's admission registration, not of any enumerated or discovered Namespace list. `cage-tier` (and `policy-version-orphan-cage`) MUST be registered with a cluster-scoped `namespaceSelector` that matches all Namespace objects unconditionally (e.g. an empty/match-all selector), never a selector or discovery mechanism that depends on an enumerated, generated, or periodically-refreshed list of known Namespaces. Any composed artefact, region, or cluster that the discovery mechanism does not enumerate is itself the loophole this clause forecloses: the webhook's registration is the only 'discovery' that counts, and Kubernetes' own admission-registration guarantees (a webhook configured to match all Namespaces intercepts every Namespace create/update, including ones outside any artefact-level enumeration) are what make 'everything is always caged' true in practice, not a maintained list. Where a cluster region or Namespace is genuinely outside the webhook's registered scope (e.g., a separate API server, a separate cluster), that region is outside the estate's admission surface entirely and must be declared out-of-scope explicitly in the platform's topology record — silence about a region's existence is not a way to exempt it; an undeclared region is a gap in the estate's boundary, to be closed by extending webhook registration to it, not a workload-level escape hatch."

Additionally add a verification/tripwire requirement analogous to `distribution/verify-infra-declaration.sh`: a periodic cluster-wide reconciliation check enumerating all live Namespace objects via the Kubernetes API directly (not via the platform's composed-artefact list) and asserting each has the expected cage-tier pod-level mutation evidence, failing the gate if any Namespace is found with no corresponding tier stamp.
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The loophole exploits an implementation detail (discovery-list-scoped webhook coverage) that contradicts the doctrine's own stated universality ("everything is always caged," "silence buys the bottom rung"). The fix mandates that admission coverage be achieved via cluster-scoped, match-all webhook registration (a property Kubernetes' own admission-controller mechanism guarantees) rather than an enumerated/discovered Namespace list, plus an independent cluster-wide reconciliation tripwire that catches any Namespace lacking tier evidence. This closes the coverage gap without altering any tier-selection, floor, infra-role, or ladder logic, so it introduces no conflict with any resolved case.
</resolution_summary>

<reasoning>
Principle 10 already establishes that tier selection is "over the party, not the price line" — the Namespace is merely where it's declared, not the unit of memory. The loophole arises because the binding check (`tier_binding.py`) keys its "no looser than before" comparison off the Namespace *object's* current label rather than the party's accumulated tier history. That's an implementation gap, not a principled boundary: nothing in the ladder doctrine says tighten-only resets on renaming the carrier object, and Principle 11 explicitly requires loosening to be priced. Recreating a Namespace under a new name is not a priced floor change — it's an unpriced reset, which is exactly what Principle 3 (no exemptions) forbids in another guise.

The fix is straightforward and consistent with existing machinery: track the tighten-only floor per **party identity** (the `platform/party.yaml`-style identity already used for `infra`-role checks and `floor` declarations), not per Namespace name. When a party declares any governed Namespace (new or renamed), `tier_binding.py`/`apply_tier_declaration()` must clamp the proposed tier to the strictest of (a) that Namespace's own price-line fold and (b) the party's last-recorded committed tier across all its governed Namespaces, however named. A brand-new Namespace name is not a blank slate for a party that already has committed history.

This doesn't contradict any prior resolved case (there are none yet) and it doesn't contradict any stated principle — it actually enforces Principle 10 more faithfully than the current code does, and keeps loosening priced per Principle 11.
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Amend the "selection is over the party" note (2026-09-04 addendum) and `tier_binding.py`:

1. Add a persisted per-party tier ledger, keyed by the party identity already used for `infra`-role and floor declarations (not by Namespace name/UID). On every accepted governed-Namespace tier declaration (creation, update, or recreation), the party's ledger entry is updated to the strictest tier the party has ever had bound, and is itself tighten-only: it can only get stricter automatically; lowering it requires the same priced-floor mechanism as Article 11.

2. `apply_tier_declaration()` / `tier_binding.py` must compute the enforced floor for any Namespace declaration as `max(rank(proposed_tier from prices[]), rank(party_ledger[party]))`, not merely `max` against that same Namespace's own prior label. A freshly created Namespace inherits its party's ledger floor as its tighten-only baseline.

3. Explicitly state: deleting and recreating a governed Namespace, under any name, does not reset a party's committed tier. Namespace identity is the declaration surface; party identity is the unit of tighten-only memory, consistent with Principle 10.

4. The binding check (`shift-left.yml` / hub `verify/tier-binding/`) is extended to look up and enforce the party ledger floor in addition to the existing per-Namespace label comparison.
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The loophole exploited the fact that tighten-only memory was keyed to Namespace object identity rather than party identity, letting a party launder away an accumulated tight tier via rename/recreate. The fix introduces a party-keyed, tighten-only tier ledger that any new or recreated Namespace declaration must be clamped against, alongside the existing per-price-line fold — closing the loophole while reinforcing (not contradicting) the existing principle that tier selection is over the party, and keeping any real loosening subject to the priced-floor mechanism.
</resolution_summary>

<reasoning>
Principle 3 bans exemptions (carve-outs for a named workload), but principle 4 explicitly endorses conditional policy as the legitimate alternative: "you may do X if you meet conditions C." The SRE's problem is not that the doctrine has no room for incident response — it's that no conditional path yet exists. That is a gap to fill, not a reason to break the tighten-only/no-exemption/fail-closed architecture.

A revision can introduce a new, generally-available declared tier — e.g. `incident` — that any party may declare on a Namespace *if* it meets objective, checkable conditions (e.g., a signed/attested incident-ticket reference, TTL bound, auto-expiry to `isolated` after the window, restricted to a pre-approved capability set like read-only packet capture with egress scoped to cluster-internal diagnostics). This is squarely principle 4/5 territory: the cage implements the control (time-bound, scoped egress) rather than a human being denied or favoured. It is not named-workload-specific — anyone on-call, meeting the same declared conditions, gets the same treatment. It still fails closed: an undeclared or malformed incident claim renders `isolated` per principle 7. It stays tighten-only in the sense that the incident tier is still a real point on (an extended) ladder with real dials, not a bypass of the cage machinery — it's priced/scoped, not free.

This doesn't contradict any prior resolved case (there are none yet) and is consistent with principles 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10: tier still attaches to Namespace, still declared not labelled, still fails closed on silence/malformed claims, still tighten-only per the ladder rank ordering (incident sits between `restricted` and `isolated`, tighter than baseline, looser than isolated but auto-expiring).

This is a drafting gap, not a moral contradiction requiring escalation — the doctrine already contains the tool (conditional policy) needed to fix it.
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Add a new declared rung, `incident`, to the ladder between `restricted` and `isolated` (ladder becomes `baseline, restricted, quarantine, incident, isolated, infra`, with `rank()` extended by one). A Namespace may be declared at `incident` by ANY party (not gated by role, unlike `infra`) if and only if the declaration carries a verifiable, structured claim: an incident-ticket/on-call-system reference, a TTL (max N hours), and a bounded capability set (e.g., read-only network diagnostics: packet capture permitted, egress/ingress scoped to cluster-internal traffic only, no privilege escalation, no host namespaces). `cage-tier` renders the `incident` cage's dials from this fixed, pre-authored spec — it is not negotiable per-claim, only the TTL and ticket reference vary. On TTL expiry the Namespace automatically renders `isolated` (the bottom rung), enforced by the same MutatingPolicy machinery, not a human action. A malformed, unverifiable, or missing incident claim renders `isolated` per the existing fail-closed rule (principle 7) — silence still buys nothing. This is a conditional policy per principle 4: identical treatment for anyone meeting the same objective conditions, no named-workload carve-out, and the cage (not a human gatekeeper) implements and time-bounds the control per principle 5.
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The case is resolved by adding a generally-available, condition-gated `incident` tier to the cage ladder — auto-expiring, capability-bounded, and verifiable by structured claim (ticket reference + TTL) rather than by anyone's discretion. This gives on-call responders a legitimate, non-exemption path to a workable cage during genuine incidents while preserving tighten-only mutation, Namespace-scoped declaration, and fail-closed defaults for any unverified or expired claim.
</resolution_summary>

<reasoning>
Principle 4 establishes conditional policy ("you may do X if you meet conditions C") as the legitimate alternative to ad-hoc exemptions — exactly the tool needed here. The 2026-09-04 note explicitly frames "loosening is not implemented" as an *interim* state pending a future ticket ("the looser path stays a later ticket"), not a permanent architectural constraint. So adding a time-boxed conditional-loosening mechanism doesn't contradict that note; it fulfills what the note anticipated.

The fix: define a conditional policy for temporary floor loosening — e.g., a signed, pre-authorized "pentest window" artefact (scope, time bounds, authorizing role, auto-revert timestamp) that `tier_binding.py`/the hub verifier accepts as a second lawful declaration path alongside the manual PR, still requiring a signed commit (per the identity-regexp discipline) and still fully auditable/open (satisfying principle 13), but machine-checked against the conditions rather than requiring synchronous human review latency. At expiry, an automated reversion (itself a signed, policy-triggered commit) restores the floor — this is not a "silent edit" (principle 13) because the trigger conditions and the revert are themselves versioned and logged, and it's not an exemption (principle 3) because *any* party meeting the same conditions (signed pre-authorization + time-bound scope) gets identical treatment.

This is consistent with: principle 11 (loosening is priced, never refused — the conditional path still prices/scopes it), principle 4 (conditional policy over favours), principle 13 (still resolved via signed, open, reviewed artefacts, just templated/automatable rather than ad hoc), and doesn't touch tighten-only cage mutation (principle 8, unaffected — this concerns floor *declaration*, not the webhook). No prior resolved case exists to conflict with (list is empty), and nothing in ADR-0022 forecloses this — it explicitly reserves the topic for a later ticket.
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Add a new conditional-policy mechanism for time-boxed floor loosening, supplementing (not replacing) the manual PR path:

1. Define a `pentest-window` declaration artefact: a signed manifest (gitsign, same identity-regexp discipline as `propose-tier.yml`) carrying `party`, `namespace`, `requested_floor`, `authorizing_role` (must be platform or designated security-authority role), `scope` (syscalls/network reach requested), `start_time`, `end_time` (hard cap, e.g. max 72h).
2. `tier_binding.py` / hub `verify/tier-binding/` is extended to accept a *second* lawful looser-than-declared state: a pod/Namespace tier that is looser than the current floor is permitted, without a human-reviewed PR merge, IF and only if a valid, signed, non-expired `pentest-window` artefact exists for that Namespace/party covering the current time and the requested scope. This is conditional policy (principle 4), not an exemption, because any party presenting the same signed pre-authorization gets identical treatment.
3. On `end_time`, an automated (policy-triggered, signed) commit reverts the floor to its prior value; this commit is itself logged and reviewable (principle 13 — "in the open," just machine-triggered rather than human-authored), not a silent edit.
4. The manual PR path from the 2026-09-04 note remains the mechanism for *permanent* or *unbounded* loosening (aggregate residual argument); the pentest-window path is strictly for pre-authorized, hard-capped, auto-reverting windows and cannot be used to achieve a permanent loosening (if `end_time` lapses without revert succeeding, the Namespace fails closed to its prior floor or tighter — consistent with principle 6/7's fail-closed default).
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The case is resolved by recognizing that the 2026-09-04 note's "loosening is not implemented" was explicitly interim, and by introducing a conditional-policy mechanism (per principle 4) — a signed, scope-and-time-bounded "pentest-window" artefact — that lets any party meeting the same authorization conditions obtain an automatically-reverting floor loosening without per-instance human PR review, while still being priced, signed, logged, and auto-reverted (never a silent or permanent exemption), leaving the manual PR path intact for permanent/unbounded loosening.
</resolution_summary>

<reasoning>
The scenario objects to identical treatment of innocent oversight vs deliberate evasion. But principles 2, 3, and 7 are explicit and absolute: there are no exemptions, nothing is denied based on intent, and "silence is not an exemption and it is not a refusal either; silence is the bottom rung." Carving out an "innocent mistake" exception — even a well-intentioned one — would reintroduce exactly the exemption concept principle 3 bans, and would require the system to adjudicate intent, which contradicts the whole mutating-not-validating design (principle 2). So the *severity of the mutation* cannot be softened for this pod without violating settled principles.

However, the actual moral complaint decomposes into two parts: (a) the outcome is too harsh for an innocent case, and (b) there's no diagnostic signal, so the engineer can't tell what happened or fix it quickly. Part (a) is not fixable without contradicting principles 2/3/7. Part (b) *is* fixable: nothing in the doctrine forbids emitting an explanatory signal (a Kubernetes Event, a status condition, or an annotation) alongside the mutation, stating why the pod was caged to `isolated`. This adds transparency without loosening the cage, without creating an exemption, and without distinguishing intent — every unclaimed pod gets the same explanatory event, uniformly (satisfying principle 4's "anyone meeting C is treated identically"). This directly addresses the "no error message... obscure label diff" complaint while leaving the substantive rung unchanged, so it doesn't conflict with the 2026-09-05 amendment's outcome.

This is a minimal, principled addition rather than a hacky exception, and is consistent with principle 13 (disagreement/fixes happen via open, reviewable change) and the overall admission-controller framing (mutation may still surface a reason, since ADR-0020's PRICE-emission refusal path already models "explaining why" without it being a denial).
</reasoning>

<verdict>resolvable</verdict>

<proposed_revision>
Amend `governed-namespace-requires-claim`'s MutatingPolicy so that, whenever it admits a pod onto the bottom rung due to a missing/unknown `policy-as-versioned.dev/policy-version` claim, it also emits a uniform, machine-and-human-readable explanation alongside the mutation — e.g., a Kubernetes Event (`reason: BottomRungNoVersionClaim`) and/or a `posture.acme.io/bottom-rung-reason: "no policy-version claim"` annotation written onto the pod at the same time as the tier/PriorityClass/hardening fields. This applies identically to every unclaimed pod regardless of apparent intent — it is not a lighter cage, not a grace period, and not an exemption; the rung, dials, eviction class and reach cage are unchanged. It only adds a discoverable, uniform reason so that routine human error is diagnosable without requiring the system to distinguish it from adversarial version-omission.
</proposed_revision>

<resolution_summary>
The harshness of the bottom-rung outcome cannot be reduced for "innocent" cases without violating the doctrine's ban on exemptions and intent-based judgment (principles 2, 3, 7), so the mutation itself stays exactly as ADR-0022 specifies. But the case's real, fixable defect is the silence around *why* — so the revision adds a uniform diagnostic Event/annotation emitted by the same MutatingPolicy for every unclaimed pod, making the bottom-rung placement immediately legible to any engineer without softening or distinguishing the underlying rule.
</resolution_summary>
